options.text: The sharing of electrons between metal and non-metal atoms
The transfer of electrons from one metal atom to another
The electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons
The attraction between metal atoms and water molecules

questions.explanation: Metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between the positive metal ions (cations) arranged in a regular lattice and the 'sea' of delocalised electrons surrounding them.

questions.stem: Why are metals good conductors of electricity?

options.text: Because they contain ions that can move
Because they have delocalised electrons that can flow through the structure
Because they have high melting points
Because they are shiny

questions.explanation: Metals conduct electricity because they have delocalised electrons that are free to move through the metal structure. When a voltage is applied, these electrons flow, carrying electrical charge.

questions.stem: Why are metals malleable (can be bent and shaped)?

options.text: Because their bonds break easily
Because layers of positive ions can slide over each other while delocalised electrons hold them together
Because they are made of soft atoms
Because they contain weak intermolecular forces

questions.explanation: In metals, layers of positive ions can slide over each other when a force is applied, without the metallic bond breaking. The delocalised electrons continue to hold the ions together in their new positions.

questions.stem: Why do metals generally have high melting points?

options.text: Because they contain covalent bonds
Because the strong metallic bonds throughout the giant structure require a lot of energy to break
Because they are very dense
Because they are shiny solids

questions.explanation: Metals have high melting points because a large amount of energy is needed to overcome the strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the sea of delocalised electrons throughout the giant metallic structure.

questions.stem: What happens to the outer shell electrons in metallic bonding?

options.text: They are shared between pairs of atoms
They are transferred to non-metal atoms
They become delocalised and move freely throughout the structure
They remain fixed in their shells

questions.explanation: In metallic bonding, the outer shell electrons leave the metal atoms and become delocalised, forming a 'sea' of electrons that can move freely throughout the entire metal structure.

questions.stem: Why are metals good conductors of thermal energy (heat)?

options.text: Because they are shiny and reflect heat
Because delocalised electrons transfer kinetic energy quickly through the structure
Because they have low density
Because they contain ionic bonds

questions.explanation: Metals are good thermal conductors because the delocalised electrons can quickly transfer kinetic energy throughout the structure when one end is heated. The vibrating ions also help transfer heat.

questions.stem: What are alloys, and why are they often harder than pure metals?

options.text: Alloys are compounds; they are harder because of ionic bonds
Alloys are mixtures of metals; the different-sized atoms disrupt the regular layers, preventing them from sliding easily
Alloys are pure metals; they are harder because they contain more electrons
Alloys are non-metals mixed with metals; they are harder because of covalent bonds

questions.explanation: Alloys are mixtures of two or more metals (or a metal with a non-metal). The different-sized atoms disrupt the regular arrangement of layers, making it harder for them to slide over each other.
